identification.summary: Fox Tempest is Microsoft's name for a financially motivated group that ran a malware-signing-as-a-service (MSaaS) operation. It did not attack victims directly. It sold code-signing for malware to other cybercriminals, including ransomware operators, by abusing Microsoft Artifact Signing (formerly Azure Trusted Signing) to obtain short-lived (72-hour) Microsoft-issued certificates [S1][S2]. Microsoft assesses it as well-resourced, handling infrastructure, customer relations and finances [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Service offered since at least 2025-05 (signspace[.]cloud first seen 2025-05-29); Microsoft began tracking the group in 2025-09 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft lists no other aliases for Fox Tempest [S1]. Fox Tempest is a service provider, distinct from its customers (Vanilla Tempest, Storm-0501, Storm-2561, Storm-0249); facts about those customers' intrusions should not be merged into this profile [S1]. The Telegram channel marketing the service was named 'EV Certs for Sale by SamCodeSign' [S1]. Sources disagree on Cloudzy's location (US-based per Microsoft's blog; Dubai-based per one secondary report) [S1][S3].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor stated in cited sources; described by Microsoft as financially motivated [S1].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft states the actor 'very likely' used stolen US and Canadian identities to obtain certificates, and assesses the group as well-resourced [S1]. No government attribution of individuals is reported in the cited sources.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and analysis of the signspace[.]cloud service, a GitHub repository, Cloudzy-hosted customer VMs, Telegram marketing and cryptocurrency analysis linking the service to affiliates [S1]. Microsoft filed a civil action in SDNY naming Fox Tempest and Vanilla Tempest, unsealed 2026-05-19 [S2][S3][S6]. Microsoft is reported to be working with the FBI and Europol EC3 to identify those behind the group [S3].

objectives: Financial gain from selling signing services to cybercriminals; customers paid thousands of dollars per plan, with higher tiers receiving queue priority [S1]. Sources cite plan prices of $5,000 to $9,500 [S1][S4].

targeting.notes: Fox Tempest's customers are cybercriminals, not end victims. Microsoft names healthcare, education, government and financial services and the US, France, India and China among downstream victims of signed malware, and says impact is global [S1]. Sectors and regions describe customer-driven impact, not Fox Tempest targeting choices [S1].

capabilities.summary: Fox Tempest ran signspace[.]cloud, a site built on Microsoft Artifact Signing with an admin panel, customer upload page and user/file database; customers uploaded malicious files and received signed binaries [S1][S4]. It obtained short-lived certificates valid 72 hours, created over 1,000 certificates and stood up hundreds of Azure tenants and subscriptions, likely using stolen or synthetic US and Canadian identities to pass identity validation [S1][S2]. In 2026-02 it shifted to pre-configured customer VMs on Cloudzy infrastructure containing metadata.json, a sample signed file and a PowerShell signing script [S1]. Customers were recruited via a Telegram channel and a Google Form in English and Russian [S1]. All signing activity used one provider email tied to few IPs [S1]. Signed payloads delivered Oyster (Broomstick), Lumma Stealer, Vidar and ransomware including Rhysida, INC, Qilin, Akira and BlackByte [S1]. Customer Vanilla Tempest had trojanized MSTeamsSetup.exe signed and spread it through purchased ads and fake download pages [S1]. Storm-2561 used SEO poisoning with fake VPN clients [S1].

campaigns.name: MSaaS offering begins
campaigns.summary: Fox Tempest offering signing services to the ransomware ecosystem from at least this month; signspace[.]cloud first seen 2025-05-29 [S1].

campaigns.name: Vanilla Tempest becomes a customer
campaigns.summary: Vanilla Tempest used the service as early as this month, later uploading trojanized Teams installers for signing to deliver Oyster and in some cases Rhysida [S1].

campaigns.name: Shift to Cloudzy-hosted VMs
campaigns.summary: Operations moved to pre-configured customer VMs on Cloudzy; an example certificate was valid 2026-02-19 to 2026-02-22 [S1]. One secondary report dates the shift to 2026-01 [S3].

campaigns.name: Microsoft DCU disruption unsealed
campaigns.summary: Microsoft unsealed the case, seized signspace[.]cloud, took down hundreds of VMs, suspended the code repository and revoked over 1,000 certificates, with support from Resecurity; FBI and Europol EC3 reported as involved [S3] [S1][S2][S5].

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated, well-resourced MSaaS operator; individuals not publicly identified in cited sources [S1][S3].
diamond.capability: Fraudulent acquisition of short-lived Microsoft code-signing certificates at scale, signing portal and VM-based signing workflow [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: signspace[.]cloud, hundreds of Azure tenants/subscriptions, Cloudzy-hosted VMs, a GitHub repository, a Telegram channel and Google Form, bitcoin payment [S1][S4].
diamond.victim: Direct customers are ransomware and infostealer operators; end victims across healthcare, education, government and finance in the US, France, India, China and elsewhere [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financially motivated criminal enabler in the ransomware supply chain; no state tasking indicated in cited sources [S1].
diamond.technology: Microsoft Artifact Signing, Azure identity/tenant provisioning, code-signing trust in Windows/SmartScreen, VPS hosting, Telegram [S1].

gaps: Real-world identities, location and nationality of operators are not public in cited sources.
Court filing and order dates beyond the 2026-05-19 unsealing are unverified; the court docket was not opened [S3].
Could not open BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek, Resecurity or Microsoft On the Issues pages directly; those are cited from search-result summaries.
Sources conflict on plan pricing ($5,000/$7,500/$9,000 in text vs $7,500/$8,500/$9,500 in a Microsoft figure caption) and on Cloudzy's location and shift date [S1][S3].
Whether the service has re-emerged after the takedown is unknown.
Full customer list and the cryptocurrency proceeds (described only as millions) are unquantified [S1].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: the relevant battlespace is the software trust chain (code-signing and reputation checks) rather than a geographic area; Fox Tempest affects defenders anywhere ransomware customers operate, including healthcare, education, government and finance [S1]. Step 3: the adversary is a criminal enabler selling signing at thousands of dollars per plan with queue priority, using stolen identities, Azure tenants and VPS hosting [S1]. Step 4 MLCOA: customers resume signed-malware delivery (trojanized installers via malvertising/SEO poisoning) using other signing sources or re-established services [S1]. MDCOA: a successor service abuses another certificate authority or cloud signing platform at scale (inference, not stated in sources). Candidate indicators: executables signed by short-lived (72-hour) Microsoft certificates, signer hashes and signspace[.]cloud from Microsoft's IOC table, trojanized Teams or VPN installers, Oyster/Lumma/Vidar detections [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: a valid Microsoft signature alone is not a trust signal; monitor for newly issued, short-lived certificates and Microsoft Defender detections for Oyster, Rhysida, Qilin and related families [S1]. Authorities: disruption was a civil court action by a private firm with reported FBI/Europol involvement; DoD cyber forces should rely on law-enforcement and DC3-type channels rather than assume a military role [S2][S3]. Mission assurance: enforce application allow-listing by publisher plus hash rather than signature validity, restrict software installs to approved sources, apply Microsoft's hardening guidance (cloud-delivered protection, SmartScreen, tamper protection, ASR ransomware rule) [S1]. Coordination: share IOCs with Microsoft and CISA-type partners and track Storm-0501, Vanilla Tempest and Storm-2561 reporting separately [S1].
